newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury's Rubin - shrewd but self-effacing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury's Rubin - shrewd but self-effacing.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, a shrewd but self-effacing former Wall Street executive, is expected to play a major role in shaping President Bill Clinton's second term economic policy.

A political novice when he joined the administration four years ago from investment bank Goldman, Sachs & Company, Rubin has proven adept at getting his way in the hurly-burly world of Washington -- from staring down Republicans in a public showdown over the national debt to jousting in private with his fellow Democrats on the budget.

Clinton on Friday announced that Rubin would stay on at the helm of the powerful Treasury. As the veteran in a new economic team he helped Clinton choose, Rubin is expected to be instrumental in crafting economic strategy for the next four years.

A multimillionaire known for his grasp of high finance and his compassion for the poor, the 58-year-old Rubin took over Treasury in early 1995 after spending the previous two years as head of Clinton's newly-created National Economic Council.

In that position he was responsible for coordinating the administration's economic policy -- a job that his low-key style proved well-suited for as he dealt successfully with some of the more volatile personalities on Clinton's team.
He had a rocky start at Treasury, confronted first by economic crisis in Mexico, then by a steep plunge in the dollar. But both eventually turned out to be successes.

After failing to convince Congress to set aside money for a financial rescue of Mexico, Rubin tapped a little-known fund at Treasury to provide America's neighbour with up to $20 billion in emergency resources.

Despite Republican charges that the rescue was only an ill-conceived bail-out of Rubin's old pals on Wall Street, it worked. Mexico has now repaid much of the money it borrowed and its economy is on the mend.
Rubin's Wall Street experience proved a plus in his efforts to revive the dollar after it hit a record low against the Japanese currency in April 1995.
As someone who once managed a currency trading unit, Rubin was well-placed to handle the dollar crisis, helping to engineer a 40 percent rise in the greenback against the yen.
But perhaps his greatest success to date was his victory over Republican lawmakers in the battle over the debt.
After Washington was pushed to the brink of default by Republicans' refusal to raise the debt limit, Rubin juggled little-known trust funds to keep the government operating.

The stand-off had little, if any, impact on financial markets -- thanks in part to Wall Street's confidence in Rubin -- and eventually the Republicans backed down, although not until after some had threatened to impeach him.

A moderate Democrat with strong ties to the business community, Rubin has forged close ties with powerful Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, convincing Clinton last year to reappoint the Republican inflation fighter to another term atop the U.S. central bank.
But he has also been a strong voice within the administration on the need to tackle America's social ills, especially those of its inner cities.

Rubin was an early and influential Clinton supporter. Along with his partners at Goldman, he gave tens of thousands of dollars to the then-Arkansas governor and the Democratic Party in the 1992 presidential campaign.

Like Clinton, Rubin has a law degree from Yale University and studied in Britain. He joined Goldman, Sachs in 1966 and ran its stock trading business in the late 1970s, at the beginning of Wall Street's corporate takeover boom.
A keen tennis player, Rubin was born in New York City on Aug. 29, 1938. He and his wife Judith have two sons.
